routes.label: Organize the groupings by the last operation

question: By inserting parentheses, it is possible to give the expression \[2\times3+4\times5\] several values. How many different values can be obtained?
solution:
Parentheses change which operation is performed last while preserving the order of the numbers and operation signs. We can record every evaluation by adding enough parentheses to specify all operations.

If the first multiplication sign is performed last, the remaining three numbers have two possible groupings. If addition is performed last, the two products are fixed. If the last multiplication sign is performed last, the first three numbers have two possible groupings. These cases give all five complete groupings:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\times((3+4)\times5)&=70,\\
2\times(3+(4\times5))&=46,\\
(2\times3)+(4\times5)&=26,\\
((2\times3)+4)\times5&=50,\\
(2\times(3+4))\times5&=70.
\end{aligned}
\]
Any fewer parentheses merely leave some of this grouping to the usual order of operations, so they cannot produce an additional value. The distinct values are \(26,46,50,70\); the repeated \(70\) counts once. Therefore there are \(\boxed{4}\) values, choice C.

edges.reason: Two-digit mental addition supports some final addition steps. A small-digit sum, decomposed computation or written algorithm also evaluates a two-step expression; Gemini incorrectly requires a specific oral procedure.
Multiplication-before-addition is an expression convention. A learner may evaluate needed products by grouping or counting without memorizing the earlier table, so preparation is appropriate.
Default precedence motivates why brackets can change an answer. Parentheses-first can also be introduced in an addition/subtraction-only expression without multiplication precedence.

Two-digit division broadens which expression steps can be computed. The precedence convention and a three-step calculation can also be practiced with one-digit divisors; the wider algorithm is preparation.
